t: LeetCode 798 — Smallest Rotation with Highest Score
o: We must try every rotation $k \in [0, n)$ and count how many entries satisfy `value <= index` in the rotated array; return the smallest $k$ achieving the maximum count. In Example 1 the counts per $k$ are [2,3,3,4,3], so the answer is 3. In Example 2 every rotation scores exactly 3, so we return 0. The constraints ($n$ up to $10^5$, values strictly less than $n$) rule out an $O(n^2)$ simulation of all rotations naively for large inputs, hinting that each element's contribution across all rotations should be handled in aggregate — a classic difference-array / prefix-sum pattern.
k: After rotating by k, element originally at index i lands at index (i - k + n) % n.
Each element contributes a contiguous (circular) range of 'bad' rotation values k where it does NOT score; flipping to counting bad rotations lets us use a difference array.
score(k) = n - badCount(k); one prefix-sum pass over the difference array gives all scores in O(n).

a.i: Directly simulate every rotation and count points. For each k, iterate over the array computing the rotated index of each element as $(i - k + n) \bmod n$ and check whether `nums[i]` is at most that index. This is exactly what the problem describes and works fine for small n, but at $10^5$ elements it does up to $10^{10}$ operations, so it only passes tiny tests — still useful as a correctness reference.
s: For each k from 0 to n-1, set score = 0.
For each index i, compute pos = (i - k + n) % n; if nums[i] <= pos, increment score.
If score > bestScore, update bestScore and bestK = k (strict inequality keeps the smallest k).
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n rotations we scan all n elements.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input.

a.i: Element at index $i$ with value $v$ scores after rotation $k$ iff $(i - k + n) \bmod n \ge v$. The complement — the set of $k$ where it fails — is a circular interval: $k \in [(i - v + 1) \bmod n,\ i]$ (wrapping around). Instead of counting points per rotation, count *bad* rotations per element using a difference array of size $n$: add +1 at the start of the bad interval and −1 just past its end. A single prefix-sum pass yields badCount(k) for every k, and since every element is bad or good for any given k, score(k) = n − badCount(k). Pick the first k maximizing that score.
s: Create diff array of size n, all zeros.
For each i with v = nums[i], compute lo = (i - v + 1 + n) % n and hi = (i + 1) % n.
diff[lo] += 1; diff[hi] -= 1 (this marks the circular bad interval [lo, i]).
Prefix-sum diff to get bad[k]; track the k minimizing bad (equivalently maximizing n - bad), taking the first occurrence.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to fill the difference array and one pass to take prefix sums.

w: In an interview, state the brute force briefly to show understanding, then derive the optimal solution: fix an element, ask for which rotations it scores, notice the failing set is a circular interval, and apply a difference array. Common pitfalls: forgetting the modulo wrap-around when the bad interval crosses index 0 (the size-(n+1) diff array plus `% n` on both endpoints handles this uniformly), using non-strict comparison when updating the answer (must keep the *smallest* k, so only replace on strict improvement), and off-by-one errors in the interval bounds — verify with a single-element check like nums=[0] (answer 0) and nums=[1] (answer 1). Edge cases include n = 1 and arrays already fully scoring at k = 0. Likely follow-ups: return the maximum score itself, handle values equal to n (element never scores), or generalize to left rotations instead of right.
